facts.statement: The staged manual describes a pre-license vision test requiring at least 20/40 vision in one or both eyes, with corrective lenses allowed.

evidence.excerpt:
New Mexico requires that you pass a vision test before you get a driver license.  This test measures that 
you have at least 20/40 vision in at least one eye, with or without corrective lenses.

facts.statement: Peripheral vision helps detect vehicles and hazards beside you while looking ahead; use mirrors and side glances as needed too.

evidence.excerpt:
This lets you spot vehicles and other 
potential trouble on either side of you while you look ahead.  You also must use your side mirrors 
and glance to the side if necessary.

facts.statement: Clear eyesight alone does not ensure accurate judgments of distance or speed.

evidence.excerpt:
Even if you can see clearly, you still may not be able to judge 
distances or speeds very well.

facts.statement: Distance and speed judgment matter when choosing merge or passing gaps and assessing a train before crossing tracks.

evidence.excerpt:
It is 
especially important in knowing how far you are from other vehicles and judging safe gaps when 
merging and when passing on two lane roads, or when judging the speed of a train before crossing 
tracks safely.

facts.statement: If night vision or headlight glare is troublesome, the manual advises limiting nighttime driving to necessity and taking extra care.

evidence.excerpt:
If you have problems seeing at night, don’t drive more than is 
necessary and be very careful when you do.

facts.statement: Wear the glasses or contact lenses you need for driving whenever you drive.

evidence.excerpt: If you need to wear glasses or contact lenses for driving, remember to always wear them when you drive.

facts.statement: Avoid dark glasses and tinted contacts at night because they reduce the light available for vision.

evidence.excerpt:
Avoid using dark glasses or tinted contact lenses at night, even if you think they help with glare. The 
problem is that they cut down the light that you need to see clearly.

facts.statement: Fatigue can impair seeing, alertness, decision speed and decision quality.

evidence.excerpt:
You do not see as well, nor are you as alert. It takes you 
more time to make decisions and you do not always make good decisions.

facts.statement: Tiredness may increase irritability and can lead to falling asleep at the wheel.

evidence.excerpt:
You can be more irritable and 
can get upset more easily.  When you are tired you could fall asleep behind the wheel and crash

facts.statement: Get your usual night’s sleep before a long trip and plan departure for a time when rested.

evidence.excerpt: Try to get a normal night’s sleep before you leave.

Do not leave on a trip if you are already tired.  Plan your trips so you can leave when you are 
rested.

facts.statement: The fatigue guidance flags medicine that causes drowsiness as a trip risk.

evidence.excerpt: Do not take any medicine that can make you drowsy.

facts.statement: The handbook advises a light pre-trip meal because a large meal can make some people sleepy.

evidence.excerpt:
Eat lightly.  Do not eat a large meal before you leave.  Some people get sleepy after they eat a big 
meal.

facts.statement: On a long trip, the source recommends rest stops about hourly or whenever needed and allowing ample time for the trip.

evidence.excerpt: Take breaks.  Stop every hour or so or when you need to.

Plan 
for plenty of time to complete your trip safely.

facts.statement: Its rest-break examples include walking, fresh air and coffee, soda or juice; these are presented alongside its separate prohibition on driving sleepy.

evidence.excerpt:
Walk around, get some fresh air and 
have some coffee, soda or juice.
Never drive if you are sleepy.

facts.statement: Do not drive while sleepy; stop to sleep rather than relying on the hope of staying awake.

evidence.excerpt:
Never drive if you are sleepy.  It is better to stop and sleep for a few hours than to take a chance 
thinking you can stay awake.

facts.statement: Where possible, another driver can take over while you sleep.

evidence.excerpt:
If possible switch driving tasks with another driver so you can sleep 
while they drive.

facts.statement: Alcohol can impair judgment as well as driving skill, including the ability to recognize when to stop drinking.

evidence.excerpt:
Alcohol affects those 
areas of your brain that control judgment and skill.
it affects your judgment and reduces your ability to know when to stop drinking.

facts.statement: Alcohol slows reactions and reflexes, impairs clarity of vision and reduces alertness.

evidence.excerpt:
Alcohol slows your reflexes and reaction time, reduces your ability to see clearly and makes you less 
alert.

facts.statement: Increasing alcohol levels worsen judgment, distance and speed estimates, and control of the vehicle.

evidence.excerpt:
As the amount of alcohol in your body increases, your judgment worsens and your skills decrease.  
You will have trouble judging distances, speeds and the movement of other vehicles.  You will also have 
trouble controlling your vehicle.

facts.statement: Even a single alcoholic drink can affect driving.

evidence.excerpt: Even one drink of alcohol can affect your driving.

facts.statement: The manual’s comparison defines one drink as 1½ ounces of 80-proof liquor, 12 ounces of beer, or five ounces of wine.

evidence.excerpt:
An alcohol drink is 1 1/2 oz. of 80-proof liquor (one shot glass) straight or with a mixer, 12 oz. of beer (a 
regular size can, bottle, or glass) or a 5 oz. glass of wine.

facts.statement: A specialty drink may contain alcohol equivalent to several ordinary drinks.

evidence.excerpt:
Specialty drinks can have more alcohol in them 
and are the same as having several normal drinks.

facts.statement: The source says coffee, fresh air, exercise and cold showers do not sober someone quickly; it identifies elapsed time as the factor.

evidence.excerpt:
There is no way to sober up quickly.  Coffee, fresh 
air, exercise or cold showers will not help. Time is the only thing that will sober you up.

facts.statement: When attending an event with alcohol, arrange a designated driver, transit or an available cab.

evidence.excerpt:
If you are going to a social situation where alcohol will be served, use a designated driver or use public 
transportation or a cab, if available.

facts.statement: Prescription and nonprescription medicines can impair driving, sometimes with effects comparable to or worse than alcohol.

evidence.excerpt:
These drugs 
can have effects like those of alcohol, or even worse.  This is true of many prescription drugs and even 
many of the drugs you can buy without a prescription.

facts.statement: Medicines for headaches, colds, allergies or calming nerves may cause drowsiness and affect driving.

evidence.excerpt:
Drugs taken for headaches, colds, hay fever or 
other allergies or those to calm nerves can make a person drowsy and affect their driving.

facts.statement: The manual warns that stimulant or diet pills may briefly increase perceived alertness but later cause nervousness, dizziness, poor concentration or vision effects.

evidence.excerpt:
Pep pills, 
“uppers” and diet pills can make a driver feel more alert for a short time.   Later however, they can cause 
a person to be nervous, dizzy, unable to concentrate, and they can affect your vision.

facts.statement: Check medicine labels for driving warnings; ask a doctor or pharmacist about side effects if unsure whether driving is safe.

evidence.excerpt:
If you are driving, check the label before you take a drug for warnings about its effect.  If you are not sure 
it is safe to take the drug and drive, ask your doctor or pharmacist about any side effects.

facts.statement: The handbook warns against combining alcohol with other drugs because their effects may multiply or add and can seriously harm health and driving ability.

evidence.excerpt:
Never drink alcohol while you are taking other drugs.  These drugs could multiply the effects of alcohol 
or have additional effects of their own.
could cause serious health problems, even death.

facts.statement: The source identifies illegal drugs, including marijuana in its example, as a driving-impairment concern.

evidence.excerpt: Illegal drugs are not good for your health and affect your ability to be a safe driver.

For example, studies 
have shown that people who use marijuana make more mistakes, have more trouble adjusting to glare

facts.statement: Illness or discomfort, including a cold, stiff neck, cough or sore leg, may impair driving; let someone else drive when unwell and needing transportation.

evidence.excerpt:
Many health problems can affect your driving—a bad cold, infection or virus.  Even little problems like a 
stiff neck, a cough or a sore leg can affect your driving.  If you are not feeling well and need to go 
somewhere, let someone else drive.

facts.statement: The staged handbook says buying, consuming or possessing alcohol is prohibited below age 21.

evidence.excerpt:
You are not allowed to buy alcohol, consume alcohol or be in possession of alcohol unless you are 21 
years of age.

facts.statement: According to the staged manual, driving with BAC of 0.08% or above can result in arrest.

evidence.excerpt:
You can be arrested for 
driving with a blood alcohol content (BAC) of .08% or more.

facts.statement: For a driver younger than 21, the handbook also states arrest is possible at BAC 0.02%.

evidence.excerpt:
In New Mexico, if you are under 21, you 
also can be arrested for BAC at .02%.

facts.statement: BAC expresses the percentage of alcohol in blood; the manual lists breath, blood and urine testing.

evidence.excerpt:
BAC is the percentage of alcohol in your blood and is usually 
determined by a breath, blood or urine test.

facts.statement: The manual says refusing a BAC test requested by a police or traffic officer can cost a driver the license for one year.

evidence.excerpt:
If a police or traffic officer asks you to take a BAC test and 
refuse to do so, you can lose your driver license for one year.

facts.statement: For a first DWI conviction, the source states fines and court costs apply and jail is possible.

evidence.excerpt:
If you are found guilty of DWI and it is your first conviction, you will pay stiff fines and court costs, and 
you could be sentenced to jail.

facts.statement: The first-conviction description also requires treatment and installation of an ignition-interlock device.

evidence.excerpt:
You will also be ordered to treatment and to install an ignition interlock 
device on your vehicle.

facts.statement: The handbook describes MVD as having authority to revoke the driver’s license after DWI.

evidence.excerpt: MVD has the authority to revoke your driver’s license.

facts.statement: The source says later DWI convictions increase fines, jail time and the length of license revocation.

evidence.excerpt:
Subsequent DWI 
convictions will result in increased fines, more jail time, and a longer license revocation.

facts.statement: The handbook states that a DWI conviction stays on the driving record for 25 years.

evidence.excerpt:
Any DWI 
conviction will remain on your driving record for twenty-five years.

facts.statement: The handbook describes driving under any drug’s influence that makes driving unsafe as unlawful.

evidence.excerpt:
Driving under 
the influence of any drug that makes you drive unsafely is against the law.

facts.statement: The medical-reporting text requires periodic physician-signed medical statements to MVD for drivers with epilepsy, diabetes, adverse heart conditions or other medical problems.

evidence.excerpt:
In New Mexico drivers who have epilepsy, diabetes, adverse 
heart conditions and other medical problems are required to send the Motor Vehicle Division periodic 
medical statements signed by their physicians.

facts.statement: The source directs readers to MVD for further information about those medical-reporting requirements.

evidence.excerpt: Consult the Motor Vehicle Division for more information.

facts.statement: The epilepsy paragraph calls for frequent checkups, careful medicine management and six months stable and seizure-free before license issuance.

evidence.excerpt:
People with epilepsy should have frequent check-ups, practice careful management of 
medicine, and be stable and seizure free for a 6-month period before being issued a driver's 
license.

facts.statement: For insulin-treated diabetes, the source cautions against driving when an insulin reaction, blackout, convulsion or shock is possible.

evidence.excerpt:
Diabetics who take insulin should not drive when there is any chance of an insulin 
reaction, blackout, convulsion or shock.

facts.statement: The insulin paragraph identifies missed food or an incorrect insulin amount as possible causes of the described reaction.

evidence.excerpt:
Such a situation could result from skipping a meal or 
snack or from taking the wrong amount of insulin.

facts.statement: While a doctor adjusts insulin dosage, the manual suggests another person driving.

evidence.excerpt:
It also might be a good idea to have someone 
else drive for you during times when your doctor is adjusting your insulin dosage.

facts.statement: The diabetes guidance recommends regular eye examinations for night blindness and other vision difficulties.

evidence.excerpt:
If you have 
diabetes you also should have your eyes checked regularly for possible night blindness or other 
vision problems.

facts.statement: The heart paragraph cautions people with heart disease, high blood pressure, circulation problems or blackout, fainting or heart-attack risk against driving.

evidence.excerpt:
People with heart diseases, high blood pressure or circulation problems or those 
in danger of a blackout, fainting or a heart attack should not get behind the wheel.

facts.statement: A patient seeing a doctor for a heart condition should ask whether it can affect safe driving.

evidence.excerpt:
If you are 
seeing a doctor for a heart condition, ask if the condition could affect your driving safely.

facts.statement: Strong worry, excitement, fear, anger or depression can interfere with driving.

evidence.excerpt:
You may not be able to drive well if you are overly worried, excited, 
afraid, angry or depressed.

facts.statement: If angry or excited, allow time to calm down and remain off the road until calm.

evidence.excerpt:
If you are angry or excited, give yourself time to cool off.  If necessary take a short walk, but stay 
off the road until you have calmed down.

facts.statement: When worried or upset, the handbook emphasizes keeping attention on driving.

evidence.excerpt: If you are worried, down or are upset about something, try to keep your mind on your driving.

facts.statement: Dialing or talking on a mobile phone can dangerously distract a driver.

evidence.excerpt:
Dialing, or even just talking on a 
cell phone, can be a dangerous distraction from safe driving.

facts.statement: Where possible, pull to the roadside before making or receiving a phone call.

evidence.excerpt:
Pull over to the side of the road to place or 
take a call whenever possible.

facts.statement: The source notes that some towns prohibit phone use while driving without a hands-free device; it does not identify the towns.

evidence.excerpt:
it is illegal in some towns to use a cell phone while 
driving unless you are using a hands-free device.
